books.section: Topic 7.5 World War I: Military and Diplomacy
United States and World War I (1914-1921)
The Progressive Era and World War I (1900-1920)

stimulus.source_note: Figures from 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 21.
stimulus.text:
| Date | American forces in France |
| June 1917 | The first American troops land in France: about 14,500 men under General John J. Pershing. |
| Spring 1918 | Germany launches offensives that bring its armies within about 50 miles of Paris. American troops help stop the drive at Chateau-Thierry. |
| September 1918 | American troops erase a German salient at St. Mihiel, then open the Meuse-Argonne Offensive with about one million American soldiers. |
| November 11, 1918 | Germany signs the armistice. About two million American soldiers have reached France, and about 115,000 Americans have died in the war, roughly half in battle. |

stem: The arrival of American troops in France mattered most in 1918 because the Allies faced a combination of

options.text: a British surrender, the collapse of the French government, and a German march on Paris in the spring of 1918
options.misconception: Britain did not surrender, and the French government did not collapse. The Allies were strained, but both stayed in the war.

options.text: a German offensive strengthened by troops freed from the Russian front and a war that had become a stalemate
an American refusal to send troops or supplies and a German naval blockade of the French coast in 1918
options.misconception: The United States sent troops and supplies to France, and Germany had no naval blockade of France. The problem was German troops on land, not a blockade at sea.

options.text: a French mutiny that ended all fighting on the Western Front and a Russian invasion of France in 1917
options.misconception: French soldiers did mutiny after a failed offensive in 1917, but France kept fighting. Russia never invaded France; Russia left the war after its revolution.

rationales.A: Britain did not surrender, and the French government did not collapse. The Allies were strained, but both stayed in the war.
rationales.B: Background from the books: Russia left the war after the Bolshevik Revolution, so Germany moved troops west, and the war had settled into a trench stalemate. Fresh American troops arrived just as Germany launched its 1918 offensives toward Paris.
rationales.C: The United States sent troops and supplies to France, and Germany had no naval blockade of France. The problem was German troops on land, not a blockade at sea.
rationales.D: French soldiers did mutiny after a failed offensive in 1917, but France kept fighting. Russia never invaded France; Russia left the war after its revolution.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what the Allies lacked in 1918. They were exhausted after nearly four years of trench war that neither side could win.
2. Ask what changed on the German side. Background from the books: Russia's exit freed German troops for the Western Front, and Germany used them in offensives toward Paris.
3. Ask what fresh troops add to that picture. Two million Americans gave the Allies new men just when Germany was spending its last strength.
Remember: fresh forces matter most when the other side has just gained strength and the war has no room left for mistakes.
